record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: Can every right-orderable group without non-abelian free subgroups be Conrad right-ordered?

evidence.quote: 2.35∗ . (P. A. Linnell [55]) Can every right-orderable group without nonabelian free subgroups be Conrad right-ordered? (cf. Problem 2.27 (iv))

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a group. A right order on $G$ is a total order $<$ on $G$ such that for all $a,b,c \in G$, $a < b$ implies $ac < bc$. The group $G$ is called right-orderable if it admits such an order. A right order $<$ on $G$ is said to be Conradian (or Conrad) if for all positive elements $a, b > 1$ (with respect to $<$), there exists a positive integer $n$ such that $a < b a^n$. The group $G$ is called Conrad right-ordered (or Conrad right-orderable) if it admits a Conradian right order. (Equivalently, a right-orderable group is Conrad right-orderable if and only if it is locally indicable, i.e. every nontrivial finitely generated subgroup admits a surjective homomorphism onto $\mathbb{Z}$.)

Question: Is it true that every right-orderable group $G$ that contains no non-abelian free subgroup admits a Conradian right order?
artifact.status_search_result: The question, attributed to P. A. Linnell, is widely cited as Linnell's conjecture in the theory of orderable groups. Recent literature (e.g., works of Navas, Clay, Calderoni, and others on the dynamics and space of left-orderings) discusses the conjecture as still open: it is known that locally indicable groups are exactly the Conrad-orderable groups, and partial progress exists for soluble and elementary amenable groups, but no general proof or counterexample for groups without non-abelian free subgroups appears in the literature.
